fatal_errors: The relevant baseline is the SLM as-printed alloy without nanoprecipitates, not cast or wrought counterparts.
HTXRD can identify crystalline phase evolution but cannot by itself resolve localized elemental redistribution within nanoscale precipitates.
The hypothesis omits the central comparison between as-printed material and material aged at 750°C for 50 h.
It does not recover the key Cr2O3-mediated mechanism or the detrimental effect of Cr-depleted precipitates and precipitate–matrix interfaces on protective-scale formation.
The claimed link to improved oxidation performance is unsupported and conflicts with the observed higher mass gain of the aged alloy.
explanation: The proposal addresses high-temperature oxidation and offers a scientifically reasonable alternative method: in situ HTXRD can track time- and temperature-dependent formation of crystalline oxides and precipitate phase changes. Complementary TEM-EDS would improve spatially resolved compositional analysis, making the experiment moderately discriminating. However, it does not reconstruct the target study. It misses the as-printed versus precipitation-aged comparison, the specified 600–1200°C and up-to-96-h exposures, and the actual SEM-EDS/XRD/Raman and oxidation-kinetics workflow. Most importantly, it replaces the established mechanism—delayed formation of a continuous protective Cr-rich scale due to Cr-depleted L12/L21 precipitates and interface-assisted oxygen transport—with generic preferential oxidation or precipitate dissolution. The sole citation concerns a compositionally different CrMnFeCoNi alloy and supports HTXRD for phase identification, but not direct nanoscale elemental redistribution in this alloy. Thus, the method is plausible as a complementary experiment rather than an accurate reconstruction.
